viewers.about: Shows the nodes of its source on a line of time, each placed by its own date fields and read in the timeline's calendar (the Gregorian unless its settings name a calendar node). A node with a date or a start is a point or a bar; a node with neither is a group label for the dated nodes under it. Make one with set_metanode (viewer "timeline", depth 2 is usual: groups, then events), then give each event a date with set_fields.
viewers.source: its subtree, usually two levels deep (groups, then events); any source works

fields.name: date
fields.about: One moment, written as the timeline's calendar writes dates: in an invented calendar its months' short names and its eras' short names ("Fir 3, 1300 YF"), and a day of no month by its name ("Year's Gate, 1300 YF"). An era left out means the calendar's quiet era. Rough dates read too: "c. 1066", "early 1400s", "the 15th century", "spring of 412" (a season the calendar names), and a span in one field, "1215-1217". set_fields asks the timeline first: a date it cannot read is refused with forms that do, and a good one is said back with checks in the calendar's own terms (a day's weekday and its day of the year, a span's length in days), and its Gregorian date when the timeline shows the Gregorian beside its own calendar. Try a form with call_plugin_tool read_date before writing many. The Gregorian calendar is proleptic: dates before 1582 are counted as if it had always been in use, not as the Julian dates many histories give.

fields.name: start
fields.about: Where a span begins (read before date when both are there). A start after its end is refused.

fields.name: end
fields.about: Where a span ends, through the end of what it names: an end of "241 BC" runs through Dec 31, 241 BC. With start, the node is a bar.

settings.about: The timeline's own settings. Leave calendar out for the Gregorian calendar; to count in an invented calendar, make a calendar node first (set_metanode with viewer "calendar", then set_viewer_settings with its definition) and name it here by its pimble: link. Dates in fields are then written the way that calendar writes them: its month names, its era's short name ("Fir 3, 1300 YF").

calendar.description: a calendar node's pimble: link; absent for the Gregorian calendar

also.description: calendars shown under the timeline's own, lined up

items.description: "gregorian", or a calendar node's pimble: link

start.description: the field read as where a span begins, instead of start

date.description: the field read as one moment, instead of date

end.description: the field read as where a span ends, instead of end

viewers.about: A calendar node: its settings are a calendar's whole definition, which timelines name to count in it. The person edits it as a form; an agent writes the definition with set_viewer_settings. Make one with set_metanode (viewer "calendar", depth 1) on a new node. Years are numbered absolutely (any whole number, year 0 starting at epoch); eras say how a person numbers them.

settings.about: The definition. Months and days of no month come in the year's order; a date on a day of no month is written with its name ("Year's Gate, 1300 YF"). Years are numbered absolutely: year 0 is the first year after epoch, -1 the one before. An era counting up names the absolute year that is its year 1 in from; one counting down names the absolute year that is its year 1 in to (as 1 BC is). With the example's eras, absolute year 0 is 1 YF and -1 is 1 BF. The leap rule is tested on the absolute year plus offset. epoch is the start of year 0 in seconds from the Gregorian 1 January AD 1: whole days times 86400 (0 lines year 0 up with AD 1; 1 January 1200 is 437925 days later, 37836720000; negative is earlier). One era should be quiet: it is left out when dates are written, and a year typed without an era is in it. set_viewer_settings asks the timeline first: a calendar it cannot use is refused with the reason, and a good one is described back (days a year, how years 0 and -1 are written, where year 0 begins in the Gregorian calendar, how today reads); check those against your own sums.

week.description: the day names in order; empty for no weeks

week_starts.description: which of week the first day of year 0 is

anyOf.description: a month: {"month": name, "short": short name, "days": count, "leap_days": days more in a leap year}
a day of no month: {"day": name, "leap": true when it is there only in leap years}

leap.description: a leap year every N years (0: never), except every M, except every K after all; tested on the year plus offset

from.description: counting up: the absolute year that is its year 1

to.description: counting down: the absolute year that is its year 1

quiet.description: left out when writing; a year typed without an era is in it

seasons.description: named parts of the year, "spring of 412"

from.description: the month it starts with, by name

to.description: the month it ends with, by name

writes.description: how a date is written: "Fir 3, 1300 YF" by default

weekday.description: the day of the week before the date

tools.name: check_settings
tools.about: Run by set_viewer_settings before it writes: a timeline's calendar and the calendars beside it must be calendar nodes the timeline can use; a calendar's definition must be one the timeline can read and write dates in, and its seasons must name its own months. A good calendar is described back: its days a year, where year 0 begins in the Gregorian calendar, how today reads.

tools.name: check_field
tools.about: Run by set_fields before it writes a date field of a node a timeline shows: the value must read as a date in the timeline's calendar (or one shown beside it). The answer says how it reads, with a day's weekday and day of the year (a span's length in days) to check against the calendar, and where it begins in the Gregorian calendar when the timeline shows the Gregorian beside its own.

metanode.description: the timeline's pimble: link (find_node or get_node gives it)

tools.name: read_date
tools.about: What a text reads as in a calendar, without writing anything: give calendar (a calendar node's pimble: link, or "gregorian") and text. The answer says how it reads, with a day's weekday and day of the year (a span's length in days) to check against the calendar. Use it to try a form before writing many dates in it.

calendar.description: a calendar node's pimble: link, or "gregorian" (the default)

tools.name: outline
tools.about: What a person opening a timeline sees, as text: every node on the line in time order, each with its first and last day, whether it is a point, a span or a bar, and its Gregorian days when the timeline shows the Gregorian beside an invented calendar; the group labels; and anything not shown as meant (a date that does not read, an end before its start).
